newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian bond yields rise, Costello disappoints.
newsitem.headline: Australian bond yields rise, Costello disappoints.

*Australian bond yields rose after Treasurer Peter Costello brought down a mild 1997/98 budget, wiping out the earlier rally to late February lows.
By Colin Brinsden
Australian bond yields spiked in immediate reaction to what was seen as a largely disappointing 1997/98 federal budget, having dipped to their lowest level since late February earlier in the day.
"It's an initial reaction to the disappointing headline and underlying numbers compared to what the market had been building in," said Karen Pringle, Treasury economist at ANZ Bank.
Handing down his second budget, Treasurer Peter Costello projected an underlying budget deficit of A$3.9 billion for the 1997/98 fiscal year and a headline surplus of A$6.4 billion.

"There has been quite a lot of positive sentiment in the market this morning on some of the expectations that had been built in last week on asset sales numbers coming though," said ANZ's Pringle, speaking from London.

The market had been predicting an underlying budget deficit of some A$2.0 billion, and some economists had even expected it even closer to balance, but more importantly for the bond market, it had been looking for a headline surplus approaching A$10.0 billion and virtually zero bond issuance in the year.
In the event the Treasury predicted bond issuance of A$6.5 to A$7.5 billion for 1997/98, little changed from 1996/97.
The Treasury said fixed coupon bonds issuance is expected to be around A$5 billion to A$6 billion.

It estimated a gross borrowing requirement of A$5.5 billion in the year to end-June 1998, although the net borrowing requirement is negative in 1997/98, with the government expected to repay A$5.2 billion of debt.

The gross borrowing requirement reflected allowance for the refinancing of A$10.5 billion of domestic debt maturities and A$200 million of foreign currency debt repayments, the Treasury said in the budget papers.

The June 10-year bond futures contract dropped to 92.250 just after the budget statement, having touched 92.370 earlier in the day in anticipation of Costello taking a stricter fiscal stance similar to his debut performance last August.

"You still have an element of fiscal consoldiation coming through, but when you compare the numbers to the budget last year, you end up with numbers which are remarkably similar," said Stephen Roberts, chief economist at UBS Australia.
"There has been no real extension of what was a very good start to fiscal consolidation since the 1996/97 budget," he added. -- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
